slo_title: Demonstrate how interfaces can be extended and used as tagging interfaces.

mcq.q: Which of the following statements is true about interfaces in Java?

options.B: A class can implement multiple interfaces
options.C: Interfaces support method overloading but not overriding

mcq.answer_text: A class can implement multiple interfaces

mcq.q: What is the purpose of a tagging interface in Java?

options.A: It marks a class with metadata but contains no methods
options.B: It forces a class to implement all methods

mcq.answer_text: It marks a class with metadata but contains no methods

What is the default modifier for interface methods in Java (Java 8 and below)?
Which keyword is used in Java to create an interface?

sq.q: Differentiate between an interface and an abstract class in Java.
answer: Interface: All methods are abstract by default (until Java 8), cannot have instance variables, supports multiple inheritance. Abstract class: Can have both abstract and concrete methods, can include constructors, and support single inheritance.

sq.q: Write a simple Java interface and a class that implements it.
answer: interface Drawable { void draw(); } class Circle implements Drawable { public void draw() { System.out.println("Drawing a circle"); } } The class Circle provides the concrete implementation of the draw() method defined in the interface Drawable.

lq.q: You're creating a file handling system where different file types (PDF, Word, Excel) need to support common operations like open() and close(). Additionally, some classes should be marked as "Secure" but without enforcing any methods. Design a solution using interfaces, including one tagging interface, and explain how abstraction and tagging are achieved through this approach.
answer: Java Code: // Main interface interface FileHandler { void open(); void close(); } // Tagging interface interface Secure {} // PDF class class PDFFile implements FileHandler, Secure { public void open() { System.out.println("Opening PDF file"); } public void close() { System.out.println("Closing PDF file"); } } // Word class class WordFile implements FileHandler { public void open() { System.out.println("Opening Word file"); } public void close() { System.out.println("Closing Word file"); } } Explanation: FileHandler is an interface that defines the abstraction for common file operations (open() and close()). Secure is a tagging interface�it has no methods but acts as a marker. PDFFile implements both interfaces. We can later use instanceof checks to identify secure classes: if (file instanceof Secure) { System.out.println("Security checks enabled."); } Benefits: Abstraction: Interfaces let you define what operations must be implemented, not how. Multiple inheritance: Java allows classes to implement multiple interfaces. Tagging: Marker interfaces like Secure enable metadata tagging without altering logic.
